entry: Stage of the English language spoken since the Great Vowel Shift, which began in England in the late 14th century and was completed by the 17th century. Texts from the early 17th century, such as the works of [[William Shakespeare]] and the King James Bible, are classed as Early Modern English. Through colonization, the [[British Empire]] spread English to Anglo-America, the [[Indian subcontinent]], Africa, Australia and New Zealand. Major dialects include American, British, Canadian, Caribbean, Indian and South African English. According to the Ethnologue, almost one billion people speak English as a first or second language, and most native speakers live in the [[United States]], the [[United Kingdom]], Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Ireland. English is a [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]] of airlines, shipping, computing, science and global communication.

Architectural movement and style of the 20th century, between [[Art Deco]] and [[Postmodern architecture|postmodern architecture]]. It was based on new construction technologies, particularly [[Glass]], [[Steel]] and [[Concrete]]; functionalism, the principle that form should follow function; minimalism; and a rejection of ornament. Its roots lie in late 19th-century use of cast iron, plate glass and reinforced concrete, which led to the first [[Skyscraper|steel-framed skyscraper]] in Chicago. The movement became dominant after World War II until the 1980s, when postmodern architecture gradually replaced it as the principal style for institutional and corporate buildings. Leading figures included [[Le Corbusier]], [[Walter Gropius]] and Ludwig Mies van der Rohe. Critics argue that its universalism and minimalism overlooked evidence of user dissatisfaction and structural problems, contributing to a backlash by the late 20th century.

Artistic movement covering work produced roughly from the 1860s to the 1970s. The term is usually associated with art that set aside the traditions of the past in a spirit of experimentation. Much of it moved away from narrative toward [[Abstraction|abstraction]]. Early figures included post-Impressionist painters such as [[Vincent van Gogh]], [[Paul Cézanne]], Paul Gauguin and Georges Seurat. At the beginning of the 20th century [[Henri Matisse]] and others revolutionized Paris with expressive works that critics called Fauvism. [[Pablo Picasso]] and Georges Braque developed [[Cubism]], and between 1905 and 1911 [[Expressionism|German Expressionism]] emerged in Dresden and Munich. The date most often given for its start is 1863, when [[Édouard Manet]] showed *Le déjeuner sur l'herbe* in the Salon des Refusés in Paris. Some critics object that its emphasis on ideas departed from traditional technical skill.

Genre of Western concert or theatrical dance that arose in Europe and the United States in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It was considered a rejection of, or rebellion against, classical [[Ballet]], and a way to express social concerns. Pioneers such as [[Isadora Duncan]], Maud Allan and Loie Fuller developed improvisational or free dance, discarding ballet's strict movement vocabulary, corsets and pointe shoes. American modern dance is often divided into three periods. In the Central Modern period (c. 1923–1946), [[Martha Graham]], Doris Humphrey and Lester Horton developed distinctively American movement styles and clearly defined training systems, and techniques by Graham and Horton are still taught worldwide. In the Late Modern period (c. 1946–1957), choreographers introduced abstraction and avant-garde movements and paved the way for postmodern dance, which rejected modern dance's formalism and drew on [[Performance art]] and contact improvisation.

Range of [[New religious movement|new religious movements]] influenced by the indigenous beliefs of pre-modern peoples across Europe, North Africa and the Near East. Contemporary pagan movements are diverse and share no single set of beliefs, practices or sacred texts. Scholars differ on whether they form many religions or one decentralized religion with many denominations. Movements range from reconstructive groups, which seek to revive historical pagan religions, to eclectic ones that blend elements of various religions and philosophies. [[Polytheism]], [[Animism]] and [[Pantheism]] are common features, and some adherents, including atheists, uphold pagan virtues within a secular worldview. Contemporary paganism has been associated with the [[New Age]] movement, though scholars note both similarities and differences. Pagan studies began to coalesce as an academic field in the 1990s.

Philosophy developed in the modern era, roughly from the 17th to the early 20th century. It is not a single doctrine or school, but shares assumptions that distinguish it from earlier philosophy. Rationalists, mostly in France and Germany, argued that knowledge must begin from innate ideas; they included Descartes, [[Baruch Spinoza]] and [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Gottfried Leibniz]]. Empiricists, including [[John Locke]], George Berkeley and [[David Hume]], held that knowledge begins with sensory experience. In the late 18th century [[Immanuel Kant]] claimed to unite the two traditions, and his work sparked German idealism, culminating in [[Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel]]. [[Karl Marx]] transformed Hegel's ideas into a materialist form, while [[Søren Kierkegaard]] dismissed systematic philosophy as an inadequate guide to life. Bertrand Russell and George Edward Moore moved toward analytic philosophy, an updating of empiricism that drew on Gottlob Frege's logic.

Russian composer and member of the nationalist circle known as The Five. An innovator of Russian Romantic music, he sought a uniquely Russian musical identity, often in deliberate defiance of Western conventions. Many of his works drew on Russian history, folklore and national themes, including the opera *Boris Godunov*, the orchestral tone poem *Night on Bald Mountain* and the piano suite *Pictures at an Exhibition*. [[Maurice Ravel]]'s orchestration of the suite later gained fame. For many years his works were known mainly in versions revised by other composers, including [[Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov]], and many have since been restored to their original forms.

Seismic intensity scale for the effects of an earthquake at a given location. Unlike magnitude, which measures the energy released at the source, it rates the intensity of shaking at the surface. Harry O. Wood and Frank Neumann developed it in 1931 from Giuseppe Mercalli's 1902 scale. Ratings run from I (imperceptible shaking) to XII (total destruction) and rely on observed effects rather than instruments. This makes the scale useful for estimating the magnitude of historical [[Earthquake|earthquakes]]. Shaking can be amplified in [[Sedimentary basin|sedimentary basins]]. The U.S. Geological Survey uses it in post-earthquake assessments.

Founder and first supreme ruler (*chanyu*) of the [[Xiongnu]] Empire, r. 209–174 BC. Modu was the son of the previous chanyu, Touman, and seized power in 209 BC by ordering his men to kill his father. He unified the tribes of the Mongolian–Manchurian grassland after Qin forces under Meng Tian took Xiongnu pasture lands in 215 BC. After the death of the first Qin emperor in 210 BC, he expanded the empire from the Liao River to the Pamir Mountains in the west and [[Lake Baikal]] in the north. At the Battle of Baideng in 200 BC, Xiongnu forces besieged the Han emperor Gaozu, compelling the Chinese court to pay tribute and form marriage alliances. Modu was succeeded by his son Laoshang. Accounts of his reign derive mainly from Han Chinese histories, which may reflect bias.

System of integer arithmetic in which results wrap around at a fixed value, the modulus. It replaces the results of addition, multiplication and subtraction with their remainders after division by the modulus. A notable property is that the final result is the same whether the reduction is applied after every operation, only at the end, or at intermediate steps. Carl Friedrich Gauss developed the modern approach to [[Number theory|number theory]] using it, in *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* (1801). Congruence is an [[Equivalence relation|equivalence relation]] that partitions the integers into residue classes, as a [[12-hour clock]] does with hours. Applications include [[Cryptography|cryptography]], such as the RSA algorithm, which relies on the difficulty of factoring the product of two large primes, as well as hash functions. Andrew Wiles's 1994 proof of Fermat's Last Theorem used connections to elliptic curves and modular forms.

Generalization of the vector space in which scalars come from a ring, not necessarily commutative, rather than a field. Like a vector space, a module is an additive [[Abelian group|abelian group]], and scalar multiplication distributes over addition and is compatible with ring multiplication. The concept generalizes abelian groups, which are exactly the modules over the ring of integers. Modules are closely related to the [[Representation theory|representation theory]] of groups and are central to [[Commutative algebra|commutative algebra]] and [[Homological algebra|homological algebra]]. They are used widely in [[Algebraic geometry|algebraic geometry]] and [[Algebraic topology|algebraic topology]]. Free modules, submodules and quotient modules are key tools for studying their structure.

Binary operation giving the remainder of the Euclidean division of one number by another, the divisor being called the modulus. For example, 5 mod 2 = 1, because dividing 5 by 2 leaves a remainder of 1. For [[Integer|integers]] the result ranges from 0 to m−1. Programming languages differ in how they define the result when exactly one operand is negative. Many languages write the operation as mod or use a percent sign. The operation underlies [[Modular arithmetic|modular arithmetic]].

Capital and most populous city of [[Somalia]], on the [[Indian Ocean]] coast. Known locally as Xamar or Hamar, it lies in the Banaadir region, which is a municipality rather than a federal state. The city has served as a port connecting traders across the Indian Ocean for millennia. It was the capital of the Sultanate of Mogadishu (9th–13th century), which controlled the Indian Ocean gold trade for centuries, before coming under the [[Ajuran Sultanate]]. In the early modern period it was considered the wealthiest city on the East African coast, with a thriving textile industry. Italian colonial rule came in stages, with direct governance from 1906. The city became capital of independent Somalia in 1960. The [[Somali Civil War]] devastated the city over three decades, and major reconstruction began in the late 2010s.

Egyptian businessman based mainly in the United Kingdom from the mid-1960s. His holdings included the Hôtel Ritz Paris, the Harrods department store and Fulham Football Club. At his death, [[Forbes]] estimated his wealth at US$2 billion. His son Dodi died with [[Diana, Princess of Wales|Diana, Princess of Wales]] in a Paris car crash in 1997; Al-Fayed claimed that [[MI6]] had orchestrated it, a claim rejected by official inquiries. Early media scrutiny of misconduct allegations at Harrods, including [[Sexual harassment|sexual harassment]] and assault, was curtailed by his threats of litigation. After his death, over 200 women made complaints of illegal activity, including rape.

Egyptian footballer and captain of the Egypt national team. Widely regarded as one of the best players of his generation, he is the all-time top foreign goalscorer in the [[Premier League]] and the all-time top African goalscorer in the [[UEFA Champions League]]. He played for Liverpool from 2017 to 2026, setting the Premier League record for most goals in a 38-game season, with 32 in his first season. He has scored 68 goals for Egypt. [[Time (magazine)|Time]] magazine named him to its list of the 100 Most Influential People in 2019.

President of the United Arab Emirates and ruler of [[Abu Dhabi]] since 2022, and de facto leader of the UAE from 2014. The UAE was a leading actor in the Qatar crisis. He opposes the [[Muslim Brotherhood]] and [[Iran]]'s regional proxies, and the UAE signed the Abraham Accords with [[Israel]] in 2020. He has been the main backer of the Rapid Support Forces in the [[Sudanese civil war (2023–present)|Sudanese civil war]]. Human rights organizations have criticized the suppression of political opposition and free expression in the UAE.

Iranian lawyer and politician, prime minister of Iran from 1951 to 1953. He led the nationalization of Iran's oil industry, which the British had built through the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, later [[BP]]. The move provoked a British-led embargo that damaged Iran's economy. His administration also introduced social security, land reforms and higher taxes, including on land rents. His government was overthrown in the [[1953 Iranian coup d'état]], carried out by pro-monarchy forces with British and American involvement. Mosaddegh was imprisoned, then held under house arrest until his death. In 2013, during the presidency of [[Barack Obama]], the United States formally acknowledged its role in the coup.

Last shah of Iran, reigning from 1941 to 1979 as the second monarch of the Pahlavi dynasty. He succeeded his father, Reza Shah, after the Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran in 1941 forced the elder shah's abdication. After the 1953 coup that overthrew [[Mohammad Mosaddegh]], he consolidated power and ruled with increasing autocracy. His White Revolution of 1963 launched economic and social modernization, and real GDP per capita nearly tripled between 1963 and 1976, though benefits were unevenly distributed. Rising inequality, repression and inflation fueled protests in the late 1970s, and he left Iran in January 1979. Within a month the monarchy collapsed, and [[Ruhollah Khomeini]] emerged as supreme leader of the new Islamic republic. The shah died in exile in [[Egypt]], where he had been welcomed by President [[Anwar Sadat]].

Iranian singer and master (*ostad*) of Persian traditional music. He was also known for his skill in Persian calligraphy and for humanitarian work. He began his singing career in 1959 at Radio Khorasan and rose to prominence in the 1960s with a distinctive style. He was one of the few singers allowed to perform publicly after the 1979 revolution. He was a skilled exponent of the demanding dastgah tradition, and his works also drew on Mazandarani, Azeri, Kurdish and Lur music. [[UNESCO]] presented him with its Picasso Award in 1999 and its Mozart Medal in 2006. In 2017 the *Los Angeles Times* called him the greatest living maestro of Persian classical music. After supporting the Green Movement and criticizing the government, he was banned from holding [[Concert|concerts]] and releasing music.

Last king of Afghanistan, reigning from 1933 to 1973. Ruling for almost 40 years, he was the longest-serving ruler of Afghanistan since the founding of the Durrani Empire in the 18th century. He expanded diplomatic relations with countries on both sides of the [[Cold War]]. In the 1950s he began modernizing the country, culminating in a new constitution and a [[Constitutional monarchy|constitutional monarchy]]. His long reign was marked by peace until the onset of the [[Afghan conflict]]. In 1973, while he was undergoing medical treatment in [[Italy]], his cousin and former prime minister, Mohammad Daoud Khan, overthrew him in a [[Coup d'état|coup]] and established a republic, ending more than 225 years of monarchical government. He remained in exile near [[Rome]] until 2002, when he returned to [[Kabul]]. He was given the title Father of the Nation.

Emirati royal, ruler of [[Dubai]] and prime minister of the United Arab Emirates since 2006. Under his leadership Dubai became a global city, and government-owned enterprises including [[Emirates (airline)|Emirates]] airline and DP World were launched. He oversaw the development of the Palm Islands and the [[Burj Khalifa]], the tallest building in the world since 2010. He founded the Godolphin stable and Darley Racing, a [[Thoroughbred]] breeding operation. In 2012 he rode a horse 160 km to take the FEI World Endurance Championship.

Crown prince and prime minister of [[Saudi Arabia]] and the de facto ruler of the kingdom. He became crown prince in 2017 and prime minister in 2022, and is the son of King Salman. His Vision 2030 programme aims to reduce reliance on oil through investment in technology, tourism and sport. Reforms have included lifting the ban on female drivers, although women's rights activists have been imprisoned. He was the architect of the Saudi-led intervention in Yemen. A 2021 U.S. intelligence report found that he had ordered the killing of journalist [[Jamal Khashoggi]], a finding Saudi authorities have disputed.

Indian actor, producer and playback singer who works mainly in Malayalam cinema and has appeared in [[Hindi]] and [[Kannada]] films. He debuted in 1978 in Thiranottam, whose release was delayed for 25 years by censorship issues. He has won five National Film Awards and nine Kerala State Film Awards, and received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, the highest honor in Indian cinema. In 2009 he became the first actor in India to be granted the honorary rank of lieutenant colonel in the Territorial Army. He founded the ViswaSanthi Foundation, which works in healthcare and education.

Archaeological site of the [[Indus Valley Civilisation]] in Larkana District, Sindh, [[Pakistan]]. Built c. 2500 BC, it was one of the largest settlements of the civilization and one of the world's earliest major cities, contemporary with [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]] and [[Mesopotamia]]. With an estimated population of at least 40,000, it had standardized baked bricks, grid-based streets and covered drains. The site was rediscovered in the 1920s, and excavations revealed a large public bath and multistory brick houses without palaces or grand temples. The city was abandoned by about 1700 BC, along with other large cities of the civilization. Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980, it was the first in South Asia to be so designated. Erosion and improper restoration threaten the site.

Qualitative ordinal scale from 1 to 10 for the scratch resistance of [[Mineral|minerals]]. Introduced in 1812 by German geologist and mineralogist Friedrich Mohs, it ranks minerals by whether a harder one can scratch a softer one. [[Talc]] is 1 and [[Diamond]] is 10. The method was mentioned by Theophrastus c. 300 BC. The scale is useful for identifying minerals in the field, but it does not predict how well materials endure in industrial settings, and it does not measure toughness or absolute hardness.
